anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical data-model and index structures do not align with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient scans, non-covering look-ups, and excess data modification work.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Hot buffer pages and their protecting latches become shared bottlenecks, causing sessions to spin or wait while accessing or modifying cached pages.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying storage layer cannot sustain the read/write volume demanded, so I/O queues saturate and latency rises beyond acceptable thresholds.

When these three root causes coincide, the database exhibits a compounded symptom set: massive full-table or non-covering index scans push large data volumes through an already undersized or hot buffer pool, flooding it with page replacements; concurrent sessions pile up on buffer-busy and page-latch waits as they compete for a handful of root and hotspot pages; meanwhile every read or dirty-page flush must traverse an over-taxed storage subsystem, so I/O latencies balloon, checkpoint and background flush cycles elongate, and CPU alternates between spinning on latches and idling on I/O waits. Response-time variance explodes, batch windows slip, and lock or log-flush queues grow even though the server still shows unused CPU or memory capacity.

Causally, poor schema and index design drives unnecessary page accesses and writes, magnifying the demand placed on the buffer cache. The inflated churn heats specific pages (root index blocks, allocation maps, monotonic insert pages), extending latch hold times. Longer holds amplify latch contention, which in turn delays page release and aggravates buffer pressure. Simultaneously, the surge in physical I/O overwhelms disk throughput, further prolonging page fetch and flush operations; this stretches latch occupancy and deepens contention. The feedback loop between design-induced I/O amplification, buffer-level serialization, and storage saturation triggers a self-reinforcing degradation that is markedly worse—and diagnostically more opaque—than any of the individual anomalies in isolation.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
